Adult individuals of Saposhnikovi shad attain a maximum recorded body length of 38.1 centimeters [Li = 38.1 centimeters], a value that situates this species among the larger members of the genus Alosa within the Caspian Sea basin. Field surveys indicate that the onset of gonadal maturation occurs when fish reach a total length of 21.5 centimeters [Lp = 21.5 centimeters], reflecting a reproductive strategy that prioritizes early investment in somatic growth before allocating resources to gamete production. This length at puberty represents approximately 56 percent of the asymptotic length, a proportion that is consistent with patterns observed in other iteroparous clupeids. The species exhibits a relatively compressed life history, with spawning migrations occurring in late spring as adults move from deeper waters into coastal and estuarine zones. Examination of otolith-based age estimates from a long-term monitoring program has provided robust data on individual growth trajectories, confirming that the ultimate length recorded in the population is tightly linked to local productivity regimes. Comparisons with the congeneric American shad Alosa sapidissima suggest that the observed length at maturation follows a predictable scaling relationship, an inference supported by the relative proportions documented across these closely related taxa.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized through examination of gravid females captured during the spawning season. At a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], each female releases approximately 33 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 33 eggs per spawning event] over the course of the spawning window, a daily rate that translates to a substantial seasonal investment. This value for daily fecundity was derived from the product of the observed clutch size and the frequency of spawning events, which together define the maximum reproductive rate. The estimated lifetime reproductive effort is considerable given the species' lifespan, and the daily egg production figure highlights the energetic demands placed on spawning adults. Studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at the same thermal regime have corroborated field-based estimates, demonstrating that the daily spawning rate is sustained over a period of several weeks. The reproductive biology of Saposhnikovi shad is thus characterized by a high daily fecundity, a trait that likely evolved in response to the high mortality rates experienced by pelagic eggs and larvae in the variable Caspian environment.

Newly hatched larvae emerge from their chorions as minute, yolk-dependent prolarvae, with the wet weight at birth measured at just 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams]. This extremely low neonatal mass, typical of pelagic-spawning clupeids, reflects the small egg diameter of approximately 3 millimeters that characterizes the adhesive, demersal eggs deposited over gravel substrates. The tiny size of the hatchlings imposes a tight metabolic constraint: they must rapidly deplete their endogenous yolk reserves and transition to exogenous feeding within a narrow window to avoid starvation. Larviculture experiments have shown that the mouth gapes of newly emerged larvae are sufficient to capture rotifers and copepod nauplii, facilitating the critical trophic switch that underpins early survival. The mass recorded at hatching serves as a fundamental baseline for parameterizing larval growth models and for comparing early life history strategies among Alosa species. This initial weight, though minuscule, is the starting point for a rapid growth trajectory that carries the fish through the metamorphic transition into the juvenile stage within the first few weeks of life.

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults in the Caspian Sea population has been documented at 469 grams [Wwi = 469 grams], a figure that corresponds closely to individuals that have reached the asymptotic length of 38.1 centimeters. This maximum body mass reflects a robust, fusiform body plan adapted for sustained swimming during extensive spawning migrations. The transition from the hatchling mass of 0.0141 grams to this adult weight represents an increase of more than four orders of magnitude, underscoring the prodigious growth capacity of the species under favorable feeding conditions. Seasonal patterns in condition factor indicate that adults accumulate lipid reserves during the summer feeding period, which are subsequently mobilized during the spring spawning run. Comparisons with other clupeids of the Ponto-Caspian region reveal that the ultimate wet weight of Saposhnikovi shad is intermediate between that of the smaller Alosa caspia and the larger Alosa volgensis, reflecting its position along a body size gradient linked to trophic ecology. This value for asymptotic body mass is an important reference point for assessing the nutritional status and reproductive potential of individual fish in both wild and hatchery contexts.

Longevity records derived from otolith annuli indicate that maximum lifespan for Saposhnikovi shad is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] when individuals are maintained at an average environmental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to 3285 days, is relatively modest for a fish of this body size and reflects the high metabolic demands and elevated predation pressure characteristic of the Caspian Sea ecosystem. The species exhibits an iteroparous reproductive strategy, with most adults surviving to spawn in multiple consecutive years, although senescent declines in condition and fecundity become apparent after age seven. The combination of a nine-year lifespan with a high daily reproductive rate during the spawning season yields a substantial lifetime fecundity that compensates for the elevated mortality experienced during the early pelagic larval phase. Field recapture data have confirmed that the oldest individuals are typically the largest, having achieved both the ultimate length of 38.1 centimeters and the asymptotic mass of 469 grams. This longevity estimate, collected under thermal conditions matching typical summer surface temperatures in the northern Caspian, provides essential demographic context for fisheries management and conservation planning for this endemic clupeid.
